newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian forces prepare for space probe crash.
newsitem.headline: Australian forces prepare for space probe crash.

text.p: Australia's army and civil defence forces were on emergency standby on Monday to deal with the possible impact of a stricken Russian space probe which could hit Australia, Prime Minister John Howard said.
Howard told reporters it was not known where the Mars probe, carrying four canisters of lethal plutonium, would hit earth but the impact was expected about 0100 GMT (noon local time).
He said Russian authorities had told Australia the canisters were designed to withstand the heat of re-entry into the earth's atmosphere and the impact of a crash.
"In which case, there would be no danger of contamination," Howard said.
"I chaired a meeting of the national security council this morning which has asked the Australian defence force ... to make preparations to deal with any emergency," he added.
The six-tonne probe lifted off from Kazakstan on Saturday evening but failed to make it into orbit around earth. Space controllers lost contact with it after a few hours.

The possible emergency comes on the eve of a visit by United States President Bill Clinton, who is due to arrive in Australia on Tuesday. Clinton telephoned Howard to tell him of the threat to Australia, which was first announced by Clinton's aides on a stopover in Hawaii.
Howard said Clinton had expressed no reservations about going ahead with his visit, which will be partly a working holiday after the rigours of his re-election.
"He's looking forward to seeing us," Howard said with a laugh. "He's pretty comfortable and relaxed."
U.S. authorities have given Canberra information about the probe and its trajectory and offered help if a clean-up operation is needed.
Australia's space tracking equipment was unable to track the probe, according to a spokesman at the Tidbinbilla satellite tracking station.
Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said teams had begun assembling around the country to implement a pre-organised emergency plan.
The director general of Emergency Management Australia, Alan Hodges, said nuclear emergency teams were standing by as nuclear fallout was considered the greatest danger.
"The radioactive material is not expected to break up, but we have to be sure," Mr Hodges said.
"The Australian defence forces are on standby, but there is no way of telling at this stage where the satellite could land.
"At this stage we are not even sure if any debris will make it to earth...We have been told it is a small satellite."
Howard said it was not known where the probe would hit Australia, but the latest indications were north-central Australia, or the Timor Sea between northern Australia and Indonesia.
"It is a very, very moving feast and we really won't know until it comes to earth," Howard said.

"If the advice that the Russians have given both us and the Americans is correct, then even if it does land in Australia, and hopefully it will land in an uninhabited part ... then there will be no cause for any concern or alarm.
"I would of course ... urge all Australians if they do believe they are come into contact with any of the debris should display extreme caution," Howard said.
In 1979, the United States space laboratory Skylab crashed into Australia's outback, causing no damage.

The unmanned Skylab disintegrated over the desert in Western Australia, near the gold mining town of Kalgoorlie, but two-metre (six-foot) long cylinders weighing half a ton were recovered from the desert.
Australian scientists pointed out that Skylab was tens of metres in diameter, compared with the Russian Mars probe which with its wings totals seven metres (22 feet).
"The Russian space probe itself is only about 2.3 metres (7.6 feet) long," said Tidbinbilla space tracking manager Len Ricardo.
